voiceover.text: Here's where we stopped, and here's the real reaction. Aluminium foil sits in copper sulfate solution, and brown copper grows on it. Zoom in to the metal's surface. Each aluminium atom loses three electrons, but each copper ion takes only two. Electrons can't be left over, and they can't go missing, so how do these two halves fit together? Let's write each half, then combine them.

A half-equation shows just one half of a redox reaction, the oxidation or the reduction, with the electrons written in. In an oxidation, electrons are lost, so they appear on the right, as products. In a reduction, electrons are gained, so they appear on the left, as reactants. Oil rig tells you which side.

Every half-equation needs two checks, the atoms and the charge, and electrons fix the charge. Take zinc. A zinc atom leaves the metal as zinc two plus, and its two electrons stay behind. One zinc on each side, so the atoms are fine. The charge is zero on the left and plus two on the right, so add two electrons to the right. Plus two, minus two, gives zero.

Copper ions go the other way. A copper two plus ion picks up two electrons and becomes a copper atom, and both sides add to zero. Now chlorine gas. Balance the atoms first. A chlorine molecule has two atoms, so it makes two chloride ions. That's minus two on the right, so add two electrons to the left. Writing chlorine plus one electron gives one chloride is a common slip, because one chlorine atom goes missing.

Some half-equations have no metal at all. This pale green solution contains iron two plus ions. An iron two plus ion can lose one electron to become iron three plus. So iron two plus gives iron three plus, plus one electron. Plus two on the left, and plus three minus one on the right, which is also plus two. Balanced.

Now combine. Electrons lost must equal electrons gained. Watch the two counters. One zinc atom releases two electrons, and one copper ion takes two, so the counters already match. Just add the two half-equations. The two electrons appear on both sides, so they cancel. That leaves zinc plus copper two plus gives zinc two plus plus copper.

Back to aluminium. Put one aluminium atom with one copper ion. Three electrons are released, but only two are taken, so one is spare. Add a second copper ion, and it's three against four, one short. Add a second aluminium atom and a third copper ion, and six are released and six are taken. Six is the smallest number both three and two go into. So multiply the aluminium half-equation by two, and the copper one by three. Add them, and the six electrons cancel. Two aluminium plus three copper two plus gives two aluminium three plus plus three copper.

Now check the result both ways. Atoms: two aluminium and three copper on each side. Charge: three copper ions make plus six on the left, and two aluminium ions make plus six on the right. Both balance. Think of electrons like money in a trade. Every electron one side pays out, the other side has to receive.

Quick prediction. Chlorine turns this pale green solution yellow brown, as iron three plus ions form. Each iron ion loses one electron, and each chlorine molecule gains two. Which half-equation do you multiply, and by what?

The iron one, by two. One iron ion releases one electron, but a chlorine molecule takes two. Two iron ions release two, so the counters match. Add and cancel, and you get two iron two plus plus chlorine gives two iron three plus plus two chloride ions. Charge check: plus four on the left, and plus six minus two on the right, also plus four.

Here's the trap. Write aluminium plus copper two plus gives aluminium three plus plus copper. One of each atom, so it looks balanced. But the charge is plus two on the left, and plus three on the right. The aluminium atom released three electrons, the copper ion took two, and the spare electron has simply vanished from the equation. If the charge doesn't balance, the equation is wrong, even when the atoms do. And never subtract one half-equation from another. Multiply, add, then cancel.

Half-equations build the ionic equation. To get the full equation, put the spectators back. Back in the beaker, the copper ions came from copper sulfate, and the sulfate ions just drift around, unchanged. Add three sulfates to each side, and you get two aluminium plus three copper sulfate gives aluminium sulfate plus three copper.

Some half-equations, like the one for permanganate, also need water and hydrogen ions to balance oxygen and hydrogen. Those need extra steps, so we'll leave them for later. But the core method never changes. Balance atoms, balance charge with electrons, make the electrons equal, then add and cancel.

Your turn. Magnesium ribbon is placed in silver nitrate solution, and crystals of silver form. Write the oxidation and reduction half-equations, and combine them into a balanced net ionic equation. Pause here to answer.

Magnesium gives magnesium two plus plus two electrons. A silver ion plus one electron gives silver. Magnesium loses two, and each silver ion gains one, so double the silver half-equation. Magnesium plus two silver ions gives magnesium two plus plus two silver. Writing one silver ion balances the atoms, but leaves the charge at plus one against plus two.

Last one. Aluminium dissolves in hydrochloric acid, giving aluminium ions and hydrogen gas. The reduction half-equation is two H plus, plus two electrons, gives H two. Write the oxidation half-equation, and the balanced net ionic equation. Pause here to answer.

Aluminium gives aluminium three plus plus three electrons. Three and two both go into six, so multiply the aluminium half-equation by two, and the hydrogen one by three. Two aluminium plus six H plus gives two aluminium three plus plus three H two. The charge is plus six on each side. Aluminium plus two H plus gives aluminium three plus plus H two balances the atoms, but not the charge.

When zinc sits in copper sulfate, electrons pass straight from zinc atoms to copper ions, right at the metal's surface, and the energy just warms the solution a little. But each half-equation could happen separately. Put zinc in a beaker of zinc sulfate, copper in a beaker of copper sulfate, and join the two metals with a wire. Would electrons flow through the wire? Why does a galvanic cell need two half-cells and an ion path?
